_meta.notes: 14 document blueprints. Keys: aliases, purpose, reader, length_words [min,max], grade_max (reading-grade target), sections in reading order {name, aka (heading synonyms), purpose, good_looks_like, words [min,max], common_failure, optional}, write_order (start where the unknowns are, summary last), reader_questions (seed for the cold-reader test), checks (machine-checkable must-haves). A check passes when ANY of its tests passes, or, for 'none', when NONE of its regexes match. Test kinds: re (case-insensitive regex; n = distinct matches needed, total = total matches needed, date = the same paragraph must also hold a calendar date, in = blueprint section names to search, first = only the first N words), items (n list items, sub-headings or table rows inside the named sections), ol (n numbered-list items), dates (n calendar dates, optionally in named sections). If none of the named sections exist in the document, the whole document is searched. A check with 'when' (regex) only applies when the document matches it. sev is error, warn or info.

decision-doc.name: Decision doc
decision-doc.purpose: Get one specific decision made by a named person by a stated date, with the trade-offs laid out honestly.
decision-doc.reader: The decision maker (senior, short on time) and the people who will carry the decision out.

sections.name: Decision needed
sections.purpose: State the decision, who makes it and by when, before any background.
sections.good_looks_like: One or two sentences: 'Decide X by DATE. Recommendation: Y.' The decider is named.
sections.common_failure: The ask is buried under history, or it asks for 'feedback' when a decision is needed.

sections.name: Context
sections.purpose: Give only the background the decider needs to judge the options.
sections.good_looks_like: What changed, why the decision cannot wait, what happens if nothing is decided, one or two hard numbers.
sections.common_failure: Project history the decider did not ask for, so the options start a page too late.

sections.name: Options considered
sections.purpose: Show at least two real options, doing nothing included, judged on the same criteria.
sections.good_looks_like: Each option gets one line of description plus cost, benefit and risk, ideally in a small table.
sections.common_failure: One real option and two strawmen, or options scored on different criteria.

sections.name: Recommendation
sections.purpose: Say which option you back and why, in the decider's terms.
sections.good_looks_like: Leads with the pick, gives the two strongest reasons and admits the biggest downside.
sections.common_failure: Hedged ('it depends') or a restatement of the option with no reason.

sections.name: Risks and open questions
sections.purpose: Name what could make the recommendation wrong and how you would notice.
sections.good_looks_like: Three risks or fewer, each with a warning sign, an owner and a fallback.
sections.common_failure: A generic list (delays, budget) that would fit any project.

sections.name: Next steps
sections.purpose: Say what happens right after the decision, who does it and by when.
sections.good_looks_like: Numbered actions, each with an owner and a calendar date.
sections.common_failure: 'Team to align' with no owner and no date.

sections.name: Appendix
sections.purpose: Hold evidence the decider may want but should not need.
sections.good_looks_like: Tables, links and analysis behind the numbers in the body, each referenced from the text.
sections.common_failure: Essential reasoning parked here so the body looks short.

reader_questions: What decision is being asked for, who makes it, and by what date?
What are the options, including doing nothing?
Which option is recommended, and what are the two main reasons?
What is the biggest risk of the recommendation, and how would we notice it going wrong?
What happens if no decision is made by the deadline?
After the decision, what are the next steps, who owns each, and by when?

checks.label: Names the date the decision is needed by
Names who makes the decision
Shows at least two options
Contains a clear recommendation
Says what happens if nothing is decided

any.re: \b(?:do(?:ing)? nothing|status quo|no change|if we (?:wait|delay|do not|don't)|cost of (?:delay|waiting|inaction)|leave (?:it|things) as)\b

proposal.name: Proposal
proposal.purpose: Persuade a specific approver to fund or allow a defined piece of work, by showing the problem is real and the plan is credible.
proposal.reader: The approver or committee, plus anyone who must staff the work or live with its effects.

sections.name: Summary
sections.purpose: Give the whole case in miniature so a reader who stops here still knows the ask.
sections.good_looks_like: Problem, proposed work, cost and time, and the request, in five sentences or fewer.
sections.common_failure: Describes the topic instead of asking for something.

sections.name: Problem or opportunity
sections.purpose: Show that the problem is real, costly and worth solving now.
sections.good_looks_like: Who is affected, how badly, evidence with a source, and the cost of not acting.
sections.common_failure: Assumes the reader already agrees the problem matters.

sections.name: Proposed solution
sections.purpose: Say what will be done and what will not, and how it answers the problem above.
sections.good_looks_like: The work in plain words, the boundary of scope, and a direct link back to the problem.
sections.common_failure: Features and tools listed with no link back to the problem.

sections.name: Plan and timeline
sections.purpose: Make the plan checkable: what happens when, and who owns each step.
sections.good_looks_like: Three to six milestones with dates and named owners; the first result arrives early.
sections.common_failure: A single end date with no checkpoints.

sections.name: Cost and resources
sections.purpose: Say what it costs in money, people and time, and what that buys.
sections.good_looks_like: A total, the two or three biggest components, the people needed and the assumptions behind them.
sections.common_failure: One round number with no breakdown.

sections.name: Expected outcomes
sections.purpose: Define what success looks like so the approver can hold you to it.
sections.good_looks_like: Two to four measurable results, each with baseline, target and date.
sections.common_failure: Vague benefits ('better efficiency') with no number.

sections.name: Risks and alternatives
sections.purpose: Show you looked for the reasons this could fail or be done differently.
sections.good_looks_like: The top risks with mitigations, and why the main alternative, doing nothing included, was set aside.
sections.common_failure: Risks that are all external, or no alternative at all.

sections.name: Ask and next step
sections.purpose: End with the exact approval requested.
sections.good_looks_like: What is requested, from whom, by which date, and what happens the day after a yes.
sections.common_failure: Ends on a summary with no request.

reader_questions: What is being proposed, and what exactly is being asked of the reader?
What problem does it solve, and how do we know the problem is real?
What will it cost in money, people and time?
How will we know it worked: which measure, baseline, target and date?
What are the main risks, and what was considered instead?
If the reader says yes, what happens next and who does what by when?

checks.label: States what is being asked for
Gives a cost or an effort estimate
Says how success is measured, with a number
Says what was considered instead, doing nothing included
Puts at least two calendar dates on the plan

one-pager.name: One-pager
one-pager.purpose: Give a busy reader everything needed to say yes, no or 'tell me more' on one page.
one-pager.reader: An executive or partner who reads for two minutes, then forwards it or acts.

sections.name: The ask
sections.purpose: Open with what you want from the reader.
sections.good_looks_like: One or two sentences that state the request or the answer, with a date if one applies.
sections.common_failure: Opens with context; the ask appears on line six.

sections.name: Why it matters
sections.purpose: Give the reason this deserves the reader's attention today.
sections.good_looks_like: The problem or opportunity, who is affected, and one number that shows scale.
sections.common_failure: A paragraph of background that could sit under any request.

sections.name: The plan
sections.purpose: Say what you will do, in the fewest possible steps.
sections.good_looks_like: Three to five concrete steps or one short paragraph. No jargon the forwardee would not know.
sections.common_failure: A list of activities with no result attached.

sections.name: Numbers
sections.purpose: Put the cost and the payoff side by side.
sections.good_looks_like: Cost, effort and expected result, each as a figure with its unit and a date.
sections.common_failure: Adjectives instead of figures.

sections.name: Risks
sections.purpose: Name the one or two things that could sink it.
sections.good_looks_like: Two risks at most, each with what you will do about it.
sections.common_failure: A long hedge list, or no risks at all.

sections.name: Next steps
sections.purpose: Show the first moves and who makes them.
sections.good_looks_like: Two or three actions, each with an owner and a calendar date.
sections.common_failure: 'We will follow up' with no owner and no date.

reader_questions: What is being asked of me, and by when?
Why does this matter now?
What exactly will be done?
What does it cost, and what do we get for it?
What is the biggest risk?
Who does what next?

checks.label: Opens with the ask or the one-line answer
Backs the case with at least three numbers
Gives a next step with a calendar date

prd.name: Product requirements doc (PRD)
prd.purpose: Align product, design and engineering on what to build, for whom and how success is measured, without dictating the implementation.
prd.reader: Engineers, designers and QA who must build and test it, and stakeholders who must approve it.

sections.name: Overview
sections.purpose: Say in a paragraph what is being built, for whom and why now.
sections.good_looks_like: The feature, the user, the problem, the target date and the owner, in five lines.
sections.common_failure: A marketing pitch that never says what will ship.

sections.name: Problem and users
sections.purpose: Ground the work in a real user problem with evidence.
sections.good_looks_like: Named user groups, the job they are trying to do, what fails today, and evidence such as quotes or data with sources.
sections.common_failure: A solution described as a problem ('users need a dashboard').

sections.name: Goals and success metrics
sections.purpose: Define how anyone will know this worked.
sections.good_looks_like: Two to four metrics, each with baseline, target and date; one guardrail metric that must not get worse.
sections.common_failure: Goals with no numbers ('improve engagement').

sections.name: Non-goals
sections.purpose: Fence the scope so requests do not creep in silently.
sections.good_looks_like: Three to six things a reasonable reader might expect but that are deliberately left out, with a reason.
sections.common_failure: Missing altogether, or listing things nobody expected.

sections.name: Requirements
sections.purpose: List what the product must do, in priority order, testably.
sections.good_looks_like: Numbered requirements grouped by priority (P0/P1/P2), each with acceptance criteria a tester can run.
sections.common_failure: Implementation detail dressed as requirements, or no priorities.

sections.name: Design and flows
sections.purpose: Show the intended experience so engineering and design build the same thing.
sections.good_looks_like: Links to designs, the main flow in numbered steps, empty and error states named.
sections.common_failure: Screenshots with no explanation of behavior.

sections.name: Launch and rollout
sections.purpose: Say how and when it reaches users and how to back out.
sections.good_looks_like: Milestones with dates, staged rollout percentages, owners, and the rollback trigger.
sections.common_failure: One ship date and no plan for what happens if it goes badly.

sections.name: Open questions
sections.purpose: Keep unresolved items visible and owned.
sections.good_looks_like: Each question with an owner and a date it must be answered by.
sections.common_failure: Questions with no owner, left open until launch week.

reader_questions: Who is this for, and what problem does it solve for them?
How will we know it worked: which metric, baseline, target and date?
What is explicitly out of scope?
Which requirements are must-haves and which can wait?
How will each must-have be tested?
What is still undecided, and who decides by when?
When does it ship, and how is it rolled out and rolled back?

checks.label: Goals carry a number (metric, baseline or target)
States what is out of scope
Requirements are prioritized (P0/P1, must/should/could)
Says how each requirement is accepted or tested
Names the owner (PM, DRI) and the status

rfc.name: RFC or design doc
rfc.purpose: Propose a technical change, record why this design beat the alternatives, and collect review before code is written.
rfc.reader: Engineers who must review, build on or operate the system, including someone who joins a year from now.

sections.name: Summary
sections.purpose: Let a reviewer decide in one minute whether this concerns them.
sections.good_looks_like: What changes, why, the chosen approach and the review deadline, in a short paragraph.
sections.common_failure: A restatement of the title.

sections.name: Motivation
sections.purpose: Explain the problem and why it must be solved now.
sections.good_looks_like: Current behavior, what hurts (with numbers or incidents), and the cost of leaving it.
sections.common_failure: Assumes the reviewer knows the history.

sections.name: Goals and non-goals
sections.purpose: Set the yardstick the design will be judged against.
sections.good_looks_like: Numbered goals, explicit non-goals, hard constraints such as latency, cost, compatibility.
sections.common_failure: Goals that only the chosen design can meet.

sections.name: Proposed design
sections.purpose: Describe the design well enough that another engineer could build it.
sections.good_looks_like: Components and their interfaces, data model, key flows, one diagram, and the reasons for the non-obvious choices.
sections.common_failure: Code-level detail with no picture of the whole.

sections.name: Alternatives considered
sections.purpose: Prove the chosen design was compared with real options.
sections.good_looks_like: Two or more alternatives, each with what it would look like and the specific reason it lost.
sections.common_failure: Strawmen, or 'we considered X' with no reason.

sections.name: Rollout and migration
sections.purpose: Show how this reaches production safely and how it is undone.
sections.good_looks_like: Phases, flags, data migration steps, compatibility promises, and the rollback procedure.
sections.common_failure: 'Deploy and monitor' with no rollback.

sections.name: Risks and testing
sections.purpose: Say what can go wrong and how you will find out.
sections.good_looks_like: Failure modes with detection and mitigation, the test strategy, and the metrics and alerts added.
sections.common_failure: A test plan that repeats 'unit and integration tests'.

sections.name: Open questions
sections.purpose: Keep the undecided parts visible for review.
sections.good_looks_like: Each question with an owner and a date; future work separated from open questions.
sections.common_failure: Hidden uncertainty; reviewers discover it late.

reader_questions: What problem does this solve, and why now?
What are the non-goals?
What is the proposed design in two sentences, and what are its key components?
Which alternatives were rejected, and why?
How is it rolled out, and how do we roll back?
What could fail, and how would we detect it?
What is still undecided, and who decides by when?

checks.label: Compares at least two alternatives
States non-goals

any.re: \bnon[- ]?goals?\b|\bout of scope\b|\bnot a goal\b|\bnot in scope\b

checks.label: Explains how to roll back or stay compatible
Covers testing, monitoring or failure modes
Gives a review or decision deadline (a date)

project-plan.name: Project plan
project-plan.purpose: Show what will be delivered, by whom and by when, with the risks named, so a sponsor can approve it and the team can run it.
project-plan.reader: The sponsor who approves it, the team who executes it, and the stakeholders who depend on it.

sections.name: Summary
sections.purpose: Let the sponsor approve or question the plan from one paragraph.
sections.good_looks_like: The goal, the deliverables, the end date, the cost or team size and the biggest risk.
sections.common_failure: Restates the project name and nothing else.

sections.name: Scope
sections.purpose: Draw the line around the work.
sections.good_looks_like: A short list of deliverables, a matching list of things explicitly out of scope, and the acceptance test for each deliverable.
sections.common_failure: Activities listed instead of deliverables.

sections.name: Milestones and timeline
sections.purpose: Make progress observable: what is done by which date.
sections.good_looks_like: Milestones as outcomes, each with a date and an owner; dependencies between them visible.
sections.common_failure: Milestones that are activities ('start testing') with no date.

sections.name: Team and owners
sections.purpose: Name who is accountable for what.
sections.good_looks_like: One accountable owner per deliverable, the sponsor, and who must be consulted.
sections.common_failure: Team lists with no accountability.

sections.name: Budget and resources
sections.purpose: State what the plan needs in money and people.
sections.good_looks_like: Total budget or effort, the breakdown by phase or role, and the contingency.
sections.common_failure: A total with no basis.

sections.name: Risks and dependencies
sections.purpose: Expose what could derail the dates.
sections.good_looks_like: The top five risks with likelihood, impact, an owner and a mitigation; dependencies on other teams named.
sections.common_failure: Generic risks and no mitigation.

sections.name: Success criteria
sections.purpose: Define done in terms someone else can verify.
sections.good_looks_like: Two to five measurable criteria that the sponsor can check without asking the team.
sections.common_failure: 'On time and on budget' as the only criterion.

sections.name: Communication and reviews
sections.purpose: Say how progress is reported and when the plan is re-examined.
sections.good_looks_like: Cadence, format, audience, and the dates of the formal checkpoints.
sections.common_failure: No checkpoints until the end.

reader_questions: What will be delivered, and what is out of scope?
What are the milestones and their dates?
Who is accountable for each deliverable?
What does it cost in money and people?
What are the top risks, and what is the fallback for each?
How will we know it is done, and how often is progress reported?

checks.label: Puts at least three calendar dates on the milestones
Names an owner for the work and for each milestone
Says what is out of scope

any.re: \b(?:out of scope|not in scope|non[- ]?goals?|excluded|will not|won't|not included)\b

checks.label: Pairs risks with mitigations or fallbacks
Names dependencies on other teams or systems
Success criteria include a number

post-mortem.name: Post-mortem
post-mortem.purpose: Explain what happened, why, and what will change so it does not happen again, without assigning blame.
post-mortem.reader: Engineers and leaders who were not there, and the future on-call person who meets the same failure.

sections.name: Summary
sections.purpose: Tell the whole story in one short paragraph.
sections.good_looks_like: What broke, for whom, for how long, the cause in a clause, and the main fix.
sections.common_failure: Starts at the root cause with no impact.

sections.name: Impact
sections.purpose: Quantify who was affected and how badly.
sections.good_looks_like: Duration, share or count of users, requests or orders lost, money at stake, and the severity level.
sections.common_failure: 'Some customers were affected.'

sections.name: Timeline
sections.purpose: Give the exact order of events so the analysis has evidence.
sections.good_looks_like: Time-stamped lines with time zone: first sign, detection, escalation, each mitigation, resolution.
sections.common_failure: A narrative with no timestamps, or a gap during detection.

sections.name: Root cause
sections.purpose: Explain why it happened, at the level of systems and process.
sections.good_looks_like: A chain of causes down to the fixable condition, and the contributing factors that made it worse.
sections.common_failure: Stops at 'human error' or names a person.

sections.name: What went well and badly
sections.purpose: Separate what worked from what did not, and where luck helped.
sections.good_looks_like: Three short lists: worked, failed, lucky. Detection and response time are called out.
sections.common_failure: Only positives, or only a list of complaints.

sections.name: Action items
sections.purpose: Turn lessons into tracked work.
sections.good_looks_like: Each action is specific, has one owner and a due date, and is labeled prevent, detect or mitigate.
sections.common_failure: 'Improve monitoring' with no owner or date.

reader_questions: What happened, in two sentences?
Who or what was affected, for how long, and by how much?
When and how was it detected, and how long until it was fixed?
What was the root cause, and which contributing factors made it worse?
What went well, what went badly, and where did we get lucky?
What is being changed, who owns each action, and by when?

checks.label: Timeline has at least three time-stamped events
Impact is quantified (duration, users, orders, money)
States a root cause and contributing factors
Says how and when the problem was detected
Gives time to detect or time to resolve
Avoids blame language (human error, careless)

strategy-memo.name: Strategy memo
strategy-memo.purpose: Choose a direction under uncertainty: diagnose the situation, make the guiding choice, and commit to actions and trade-offs.
strategy-memo.reader: Executives and team leads who must agree, fund and act on the direction.

sections.name: Bottom line
sections.purpose: Give the direction and the ask before the argument.
sections.good_looks_like: The choice in one sentence, the two reasons that carry it, and what you need from the reader.
sections.common_failure: A topic description with no position.

sections.name: Diagnosis
sections.purpose: Name the core problem or opportunity, not the list of symptoms.
sections.good_looks_like: A short, evidenced account of what is going on and the one or two forces that matter most.
sections.common_failure: A tour of every issue with no ranking.

sections.name: Strategic choice
sections.purpose: State the choice that answers the diagnosis.
sections.good_looks_like: One clear approach, why it beats the obvious alternatives, and the assumption it rests on.
sections.common_failure: Goals and aspirations instead of a choice.

sections.name: Actions
sections.purpose: Show the moves that put the choice into effect.
sections.good_looks_like: Three to six actions that reinforce each other, each with an owner and a first date.
sections.common_failure: A wish list that does not follow from the choice.

sections.name: Trade-offs
sections.purpose: Make the sacrifice explicit; a strategy that costs nothing is not a choice.
sections.good_looks_like: What we stop, delay or decline, and who will be unhappy about it.
sections.common_failure: Nothing is given up, so nothing was chosen.

sections.name: Risks and signals
sections.purpose: Say how you will find out early if the choice is wrong.
sections.good_looks_like: Key assumptions, the signals that would contradict them, and the review date.
sections.common_failure: Risks listed with no trigger for revisiting the choice.

sections.name: Decisions and timing
sections.purpose: Close with what is needed and when.
sections.good_looks_like: The decisions requested, the resources, the first review date.
sections.common_failure: Ends without a request.

reader_questions: What is the recommended direction, in one sentence?
What is the diagnosis: the core problem or opportunity?
What are we choosing to do, and what are we choosing not to do?
How do the actions follow from the diagnosis?
What would change our mind, and which signals will we watch?
What is being asked of the reader, and by when?

checks.label: States the strategic choice in plain words
Says what we will NOT do (the trade-off)

any.re: \b(?:we will not|we won't|we are not|we're not|not doing|stop(?:ping)?|deprioriti[sz]\w*|say no to|out of scope|instead of|at the expense of|trade[- ]?offs?|give up|sacrific\w+)\b

checks.label: Names signals that would show it is working, or not
Gives a date for the decision or the first review
Diagnosis cites at least two numbers

business-case.name: Business case
business-case.purpose: Justify spending money or people on one option by weighing costs, benefits and risk against doing nothing.
business-case.reader: A finance-minded approver who will test the numbers and the assumptions.

sections.name: Executive summary
sections.purpose: Give the approver the decision and the numbers first.
sections.good_looks_like: The request, total cost, main benefit, payback or return, and the recommendation, in a short paragraph.
sections.common_failure: Benefits without cost.

sections.name: Problem or opportunity
sections.purpose: Show what is at stake if nothing changes.
sections.good_looks_like: The problem in business terms, the size of it in money or time, and why now.
sections.common_failure: A technical description with no business consequence.

sections.name: Options
sections.purpose: Compare real options on the same basis, doing nothing included.
sections.good_looks_like: The baseline (do nothing), two or more options, and a one-line reason each was kept or dropped.
sections.common_failure: Only the preferred option is analyzed.

sections.name: Costs
sections.purpose: State what the preferred option costs, one-off and recurring.
sections.good_looks_like: Line items with amounts and timing, internal effort priced, and contingency shown separately.
sections.common_failure: Omits recurring or internal costs.

sections.name: Benefits
sections.purpose: State what the option returns and when.
sections.good_looks_like: Each benefit as a figure, how it is measured, who owns realizing it, and when it starts.
sections.common_failure: Soft benefits counted as hard savings.

sections.name: Financial summary
sections.purpose: Put cost and benefit on one timeline and give the headline metric.
sections.good_looks_like: Yearly cash flow table, payback period, ROI or NPV with the discount rate, and the time horizon.
sections.common_failure: A return figure with no timeline or method.

sections.name: Assumptions and risks
sections.purpose: Show which assumptions drive the answer and what happens if they fail.
sections.good_looks_like: The three assumptions that move the result most, a downside case, and the break-even point.
sections.common_failure: Assumptions buried in a spreadsheet nobody opens.

sections.name: Recommendation and next steps
sections.purpose: Close with the exact approval and the first steps.
sections.good_looks_like: The approval requested, who decides, by which date, and the first three actions.
sections.common_failure: Ends on a summary with no request.

reader_questions: What is being requested (money, people, time), and for what?
What happens if we do nothing?
What are the total costs, one-off and recurring?
What are the benefits, how are they measured, and when do they arrive?
What is the payback or return, and which assumptions drive it most?
What is the downside case, and what would we lose?
What decision is needed, from whom, by when?

checks.label: Costs are given as figures (at least two)
Includes a do-nothing baseline

any.re: \b(?:do(?:ing)? nothing|status quo|baseline|current state|no action|business as usual|as[- ]is)\b

checks.label: Gives payback, ROI, NPV or break-even
Lists the assumptions behind the numbers
States the time horizon of the numbers
Shows a downside or sensitivity case
Says by when the decision is needed

meeting-brief.name: Meeting brief
meeting-brief.purpose: Make a meeting worth holding: everyone knows the goal, the decisions needed, what to read first and who does what.
meeting-brief.reader: Attendees who will skim it two minutes before the meeting starts.

sections.name: Purpose and outcome
sections.purpose: Say why the meeting exists and what must be true when it ends.
sections.good_looks_like: One sentence on purpose and one on the outcome, phrased as a result: 'Leave with X decided'.
sections.common_failure: A topic ('Q3 planning') with no outcome.

sections.name: Attendees and roles
sections.purpose: Show who is needed and what each person is there to do.
sections.good_looks_like: Names with roles: decider, presenter, note taker, input needed.
sections.common_failure: A guest list with no roles.

sections.name: Agenda
sections.purpose: Give every item a time box, an owner and a type: inform, discuss or decide.
sections.good_looks_like: Three to five items adding up to the meeting length, decisions placed early.
sections.common_failure: A topic list with no times.

sections.name: Background and pre-reads
sections.purpose: Give only what attendees must know before they arrive.
sections.good_looks_like: Two or three links with a one-line reason each and the minutes they take to read.
sections.common_failure: A folder of documents with no guidance.

sections.name: Decisions and questions
sections.purpose: Turn the discussion into the specific questions to settle.
sections.good_looks_like: Each question phrased so the answer is yes, no or a named choice, with the recommended answer.
sections.common_failure: Open-ended topics that will run over.

sections.name: After the meeting
sections.purpose: Say where decisions and actions will be recorded and by whom.
sections.good_looks_like: Who sends notes, by when, and the format for actions (owner and date).
sections.common_failure: Nobody records the outcome.

reader_questions: Why is this meeting happening, and what must be true when it ends?
What decisions or questions must be settled?
What is my role, and what should I prepare?
How long does each agenda item get?
What should I read before I arrive?
Where will decisions and actions be recorded?

checks.label: States the outcome or the decision wanted

any.re: \b(?:by the end|at the end of (?:this|the) meeting|outcomes?|decid\w+|decision|goal|objective|purpose|agree on|leave with)\b

checks.label: Agenda items carry time allocations
Names who leads the meeting and who presents
Gives the meeting date or time
Says what to read or prepare beforehand

any.re: \b(?:pre[- ]?reads?|read before|please read|prepare|come prepared|bring|before the meeting|in advance)\b

sop.name: SOP or how-to
sop.purpose: Let a competent newcomer complete a recurring task correctly and alone, the same way every time.
sop.reader: Someone doing the task for the first time, maybe under time pressure, with nobody to ask.

sections.name: Purpose and scope
sections.purpose: Say when to use this procedure and when not to.
sections.good_looks_like: The task in one line, the trigger that starts it, and what it does not cover.
sections.common_failure: A history of why the process exists.

sections.name: Before you start
sections.purpose: List everything needed so nobody stops at step 4 to find access.
sections.good_looks_like: Access, tools, inputs and approvals as a checklist, plus the time the task takes.
sections.common_failure: Assumed access discovered mid-task.

sections.name: Steps
sections.purpose: Give the exact actions in the order they happen.
sections.good_looks_like: Numbered steps, each starting with a verb and doing one thing, with the exact command, button or value.
sections.common_failure: Steps that combine several actions or hide a decision.

sections.name: Check the result
sections.purpose: Let the reader confirm success without asking anyone.
sections.good_looks_like: The observable result: what they should see, where, and a value or screenshot to compare.
sections.common_failure: The procedure ends at the last click with no proof.

sections.name: If something goes wrong
sections.purpose: Cover the failures that actually happen and the way out.
sections.good_looks_like: Symptom, cause and fix for the top failures, how to undo the change, and who to contact.
sections.common_failure: No escalation path, so the newcomer improvises.

sections.name: Owner and review
sections.purpose: Say who keeps this current so it does not rot.
sections.good_looks_like: Owner, last review date, next review date.
sections.common_failure: No owner; the steps drift from reality.

reader_questions: When should I use this procedure, and when should I not?
What do I need (access, tools, information) before step 1?
Walk me through the steps in order: is any step unclear or missing?
How do I know it worked?
What do I do if a step fails, and who do I contact?
Who owns this document, and when was it last reviewed?

checks.label: Steps are a numbered list (at least three)
Says how to confirm the result

any.re: \b(?:you should see|expected (?:result|output)|verify|confirm(?:ed)?|check that|you will see|success looks like|it worked|done when|should (?:show|display|read))\b

checks.label: Says who to contact or what to do when it fails
Gives an owner and a last-reviewed date
Lists what is needed before step 1

any.re: \b(?:prerequisites?|before you (?:start|begin)|you(?:'ll| will) need|requirements?|access to|make sure you have)\b

policy.name: Policy
policy.purpose: State binding rules clearly enough to follow and to enforce: what applies to whom, what is required, what happens otherwise.
policy.reader: People who must comply, the manager who enforces it, and an auditor who tests it.

sections.name: Purpose
sections.purpose: Say what the policy protects or achieves in one short paragraph.
sections.good_looks_like: The risk or goal behind the rules, and the principle in a sentence.
sections.common_failure: A history of the company.

sections.name: Scope
sections.purpose: Say exactly who and what the policy covers.
sections.good_looks_like: Roles, locations, systems and situations included, and what is explicitly excluded.
sections.common_failure: 'All employees' when contractors and vendors are also covered.

sections.name: Definitions
sections.purpose: Fix the meaning of any term the rules depend on.
sections.good_looks_like: Each defined term used later in the rules, in alphabetical order.
sections.common_failure: Defines everyday words and misses the ones that decide edge cases.

sections.name: Rules
sections.purpose: State what people must and must not do.
sections.good_looks_like: Numbered rules using must / must not, each one testable, each with a short reason.
sections.common_failure: Soft wording ('try to') that cannot be enforced.

sections.name: Roles and responsibilities
sections.purpose: Say who is accountable for what.
sections.good_looks_like: Each role with its duties: owner, approver, employees, managers, the enforcing function.
sections.common_failure: Responsibilities assigned to 'the business'.

sections.name: Exceptions
sections.purpose: Say how to ask for an exception and who can grant it.
sections.good_looks_like: Who approves, what must be submitted, how long approval lasts, how exceptions are logged.
sections.common_failure: No route, so people break the rule quietly.

sections.name: Compliance and consequences
sections.purpose: Say how compliance is checked and what follows a breach.
sections.good_looks_like: How it is monitored, how to report a concern, and the range of consequences.
sections.common_failure: Threats with no process.

sections.name: Ownership and review
sections.purpose: Show the document is controlled and current.
sections.good_looks_like: Owner, approver, version, effective date, next review date, related documents.
sections.common_failure: No effective date, so nobody knows which version applies.

reader_questions: Who does this apply to, and who is exempt?
What exactly is required or forbidden, in three concrete examples?
Who is responsible for what?
How do I request an exception, and who approves it?
What happens if someone does not comply?
Who owns this policy, when does it take effect, and when is it next reviewed?

checks.label: Gives an effective date
Names the policy owner or approver
Says when the policy is next reviewed
Uses must / must not / shall for real requirements (at least three)

any.re: \b(?:must not|must|shall not|shall|is required to|are required to|may not|is prohibited|are prohibited)\b

checks.label: Explains how to request an exception
States the consequence of non-compliance
Avoids soft wording that cannot be enforced (try to, where possible)
none: \b(?:try to|should attempt|where possible|as appropriate|when appropriate|if feasible|reasonable efforts?|best efforts?)\b

report.name: Report or analysis
report.purpose: Report what was found and what it means: the answer first, then the evidence and the method behind it.
report.reader: A decision maker who wants the answer, and a skeptic who will test how you got it.

sections.name: Key findings
sections.purpose: Give the answer before the evidence.
sections.good_looks_like: The three to five findings that matter most, each a full sentence with its number, and the confidence.
sections.common_failure: A description of what the report contains.

sections.name: Question and scope
sections.purpose: Say what question the work answers and what it leaves out.
sections.good_looks_like: The question in one sentence, why it matters, and the boundaries of the study.
sections.common_failure: Background on the topic instead of the question.

sections.name: Method and data
sections.purpose: Let a skeptic judge whether the findings can be trusted.
sections.good_looks_like: Data sources with dates and sizes, filters and definitions, and how each number was computed.
sections.common_failure: 'We analyzed the data' with no source or period.

sections.name: Findings
sections.purpose: Present the evidence behind each key finding.
sections.good_looks_like: One subsection per finding, leading with the claim, then the chart or table, then what it means.
sections.common_failure: Charts without a claim; the reader must infer the point.

sections.name: Limitations
sections.purpose: Say where the findings may be wrong.
sections.good_looks_like: Gaps in the data, biases, what was not tested, and how each could change the conclusion.
sections.common_failure: Missing, or generic ('more research is needed').

sections.name: Recommendations
sections.purpose: Turn findings into actions.
sections.good_looks_like: Each recommendation tied to a finding, with an owner and a first step.
sections.common_failure: Recommendations that do not follow from the findings.

sections.name: Appendix
sections.purpose: Hold detail a skeptic may want to check.
sections.good_looks_like: Full tables, definitions and calculation notes, each referenced from the body.
sections.common_failure: Essential evidence moved here so the body looks short.

reader_questions: What is the single most important finding, and how confident is the author?
What question was this report trying to answer?
Where does the data come from, over what period, and how many cases?
What could make these findings wrong (limitations, biases, missing data)?
Which numbers are measured and which are estimates, and what is the source of each?
What does the author recommend, and what evidence supports it?

checks.label: Explains the method and data source
Says the period the data covers (dates)
Names limitations or caveats

any.re: \b(?:limitations?|caveats?|bias\w*|small sample|uncertain\w*|margin of error|confidence interval|we could not|we were unable|does not (?:prove|show)|cannot be sure)\b

checks.label: Says what to do with the findings
Gives the sample size or record count

status-launch.name: Status or launch doc
status-launch.purpose: Tell stakeholders in under two minutes where things stand, what changed, what is at risk and what you need from them.
status-launch.reader: Sponsors and dependent teams who skim many updates and act only on exceptions.

sections.name: Status
sections.purpose: Open with the overall state and the date it is true.
sections.good_looks_like: One word (green, amber, red) or phrase (on track, at risk) with an as-of date and one sentence of why.
sections.common_failure: 'Good progress' with no status and no date.

sections.name: Progress
sections.purpose: Show what changed since the last update.
sections.good_looks_like: Three to five results phrased as outcomes, each with a number or a link.
sections.common_failure: A list of activities, not results.

sections.name: Next
sections.purpose: Say what happens before the next update.
sections.good_looks_like: The next milestone with a date, and the two or three things that will move it.
sections.common_failure: Vague intentions with no dates.

sections.name: Risks and blockers
sections.purpose: Surface what threatens the dates before it hits them.
sections.good_looks_like: Each risk with impact, owner, mitigation and the date it becomes a problem.
sections.common_failure: Risks softened until nobody notices them.

sections.name: Asks
sections.purpose: Say exactly what you need from the reader.
sections.good_looks_like: Each ask names a person, the decision or help needed, and a date. 'None this week' is a valid answer.
sections.common_failure: Asks hidden inside the narrative.

sections.name: Launch readiness
sections.purpose: For launches: show whether the go/no-go criteria are met.
sections.good_looks_like: A short checklist of criteria, each with a status and an owner.
sections.common_failure: A checklist with no owner or evidence.

sections.name: Rollout and rollback
sections.purpose: For launches: describe the rollout stages, the communications and the way back.
sections.good_looks_like: Stages with dates and percentages, who is told what and when, and the rollback trigger and steps.
sections.common_failure: Rollout without a rollback.

reader_questions: What is the overall status (on track, at risk, off track), as of what date?
What changed since the last update?
What is next, and when is the next milestone?
What is at risk or blocked, and what is the plan?
What do you need from me, and by when?
For a launch: what are the go/no-go criteria, and how do we roll back?

checks.label: Opens with an overall status (green, amber, red, on track, at risk)
Says the date the status is as of
Names the next milestone with a date
States the asks, or says there are none
For a launch: says how to roll back
For a launch: lists go/no-go criteria
